a.q: What does a sensible decision maker do when choosing between options?
opts: Picks the option with the greatest net benefit
Picks the option with the greatest benefits
Picks the option with the lowest price
Picks the option that most people choose
a.why: A sensible choice compares benefits with costs and takes the greatest net benefit. Choosing the greatest benefits alone is tempting, but it ignores costs, and an option with big benefits can still have bigger costs.
a.clue: Look at both what an option gives and what it takes.

b.q: Liam in Ballarat can buy only one: a concert ticket for $100, worth $120 to him, or a video game for $50, worth $90 to him. Which has the greatest net benefit?
opts: The game, with a net benefit of $40
The concert, with a net benefit of $120
The concert, with a net benefit of $20
Either, as both have a net benefit above $0
b.why: Net benefit is benefits minus costs: the concert gives $120 − $100 = $20 and the game gives $90 − $50 = $40, so the game is the better choice. Picking the concert because $120 is the biggest number is tempting, but that ignores its $100 cost.
b.clue: Take each option's cost away from its benefit, then compare.

a.q: What does a sensible decision maker do when choosing between options?
opts: Picks the option with the greatest net benefit
Picks the option with the greatest benefits
Picks the option with the lowest price
Picks the option that most people choose
a.why: A sensible choice compares benefits with costs and takes the greatest net benefit. Choosing the greatest benefits alone is tempting, but it ignores costs, and an option with big benefits can still have bigger costs.
a.clue: Look at both what an option gives and what it takes.

b.q: Mia in Dubbo can spend Saturday at a job that pays $80 or at a footy clinic. She values the clinic at the equivalent of $60 and it costs her $10 to enter. Which choice has the greatest net benefit?
opts: The job, because giving up the clinic costs her less
The clinic, because it has no opportunity cost
The job, because $80 is more than $60
The clinic, because she enjoys it more than work
b.why: The job gives $80 and its opportunity cost is the clinic's $60 benefit, so the net benefit is $20. The clinic gives $60 but costs $10 plus the $80 job given up, so it is a loss. Comparing only $80 with $60 is tempting, but it leaves out the costs.
b.clue: Count the opportunity cost of each option as a cost.

a.best: Picks the option with the greatest net benefit

b.best: The job, because giving up the clinic costs her less
also_right: The job, because $80 is more than $60

problems.detail: The distractor 'The job, because $80 is more than $60' picks the right option for a valid reason. The clinic also has a $10 entry cost, so $80 > $60 is enough to show the job has the greater net benefit. Two options name the job and both can be defended, so the question does not test whether students include opportunity cost.

Why (b) gives the job's opportunity cost as the clinic's $60 benefit, so it gets a net benefit of $20. If Mia takes the job she also avoids the $10 entry fee, so the next best option given up is worth $60 − $10 = $50, and the job's net benefit is $30. The why ignores the entry fee here but counts it for the clinic.
'She values the clinic at the equivalent of $60' does not say whether the $60 is before or after the $10 entry fee. This makes the opportunity-cost arithmetic unclear.

check.summary: Question a is fine. In question b, the distractor 'The job, because $80 is more than $60' is also defensibly right, and the why miscounts the job's opportunity cost as $60 when it should be $50 once the $10 entry fee is netted off.
